You decline with a bow. The herald is very good about it. The crowd groans in a friendly way, and you are somehow more respected for having been asked.
You send a student instead, who is not ready, and does very well. You get all the credit and none of the blisters, and you know it is not quite honest.

events.text: At the Crane Cup, an old fighter makes the entry that everyone knew they would, and loses in the first round to someone half their age, and bows with a courtesy that breaks the heart a little. The gallery stands. It is not a custom here, standing, and they all do it. You find you are standing too.

choices.text: Wait for them at the gate

effects.log: You wait for them at the gate, and walk them down the white stairs. They do not say much. At the bottom they thank you, and it is for something that happened centuries ago, which you had forgotten.
You leave them their dignity, and go and stand somewhere else. The gesture is understood, and you know it is, and it is quite enough.

choices.text: Challenge the one who beat them

effects.log: You find the one who beat them and ask for a bout on behalf of the old fighter's. It is a fine fight, and it is not quite the right thing to have done, and it is done.

events.text: You study the bracket of the Crane Cup the way one reads a map before a long road: who meets whom, and when, and who will be tired. The riders themselves, who vote by raising a feather have been, you see, kind to somebody and not to somebody else, and the kindness has a shape. It is quite clever. It is just a little too clever to be an accident.

choices.text: Point it out to someone who matters

effects.log: You point it out to someone who matters, discreetly. A week later the bracket is redrawn, with great ceremony and no explanation. You are not thanked and do not need to be.
You use it. It is not dishonest, exactly, to know the shape of a thing. By the end you are two rounds further than your name would have taken you, and you are not quite proud.
You let it be. Some things on the isles are as old as the isles, and a kind of fairness runs through them sideways. You find that restful, oddly.

events.text: The night before the Crane Cup, the lamps are lit along the lane to the ring, and children, mostly, who keep score on their fingers come out to see the fighters walk it. It is called the Walk, and nobody fights on it. You walk it, with a very plain face, and a girl on the rail holds up a paper crane with your name misspelled on its wing.

effects.log: You take the crane. It is a poor crane and the spelling is dreadful. It sits on your shelf for a thousand years, and you never once correct it.

choices.text: Sign it, and give it back

effects.log: You sign it, and give it back, and she holds it above her head as if she had won the Tournament. You hear about it for weeks afterwards from people who were not even there.

events.text: There are three names above yours on the Jade Register now, and then two, and then one. People have started to lower their voices when they pass the white pillar at the foot of the Stairs, which is how you learn what the top feels like. The Keeper of the Pillar, who has not left the pillar in four hundred years, now bows to you first. Nobody warned you that the air was this thin.

effects.log: You enjoy it. It is cold and clear and the view from here is long; you will remember it with something between love and fear.

choices.text: Go down and be among the middle names

effects.log: You go down and sit among the middle names for a season. They are warm and funny and slightly afraid of you, and you leave grateful and a little ashamed.

events.text: The name directly above yours on the Jade Register is an immortal of enormous age, who sends you a short note: tea, at the third hour, bring nothing. Clerks of the Ministries notice the note, as they notice everything. When you arrive, the old one is alone and pouring, and does not look up for the full length of the first cup.

effects.log: You wait. Eventually they say they are tired, that the place above you is not what it was, and that they would like to see who is going to have it. It is not a threat. It is nearly a blessing.
You ask what they want. They look at you for a long time and say, mildly, that nobody has asked that in four hundred years. They tell you, and it is smaller than you feared.

choices.text: Offer them the place without a fight

effects.log: You offer them the place without a fight. They laugh until they cough. They decline, and tell you, kindly, that you have just passed a test you did not know was set.

events.text: Every week now, at the white pillar at the foot of the Stairs, someone comes with a polite note and a new technique. The Jade Register has made you a landmark, something to be climbed, and the young are very energetic about climbing. This week it is a youth with a sword wrapped in grey cloth and a sad, patient face.

ok.log: You take the youth on, and it is over quickly and kindly, and they thank you with real warmth. They will be better for it. You are not sure you are.

fail.log: The youth surprises you, and you spend a week with an iced cloth on your arm, and a clearer sense of how long you have been on top.

effects.log: You hand them to a student, who is thrilled. It goes fine, and teaches both of them something, and spares you an afternoon.
You offer them a year in your house, to learn, with no fight. They take it, shocked, and you gain a student with a very patient face.

events.text: To be near the top of the Jade Register is to be a place worth taking, and not everyone takes it kindly. A note comes with no name on it, only a bruise-coloured seal, and the line: 'Defend it, or give it up, before the new moon.' clerks of the Ministries are already guessing who sent it.

ok.log: You defend it, in the open, against whoever comes. It is the old kind of fight, honest and tiring, and you win it. You never learn who sent the note, and you suspect nobody did.

fail.log: You defend it, and it is a near thing, and you win nothing and lose a good deal of skin. The note was real, and the sender was serious.

effects.log: You give it up gracefully, and step down a place, and are surprised how light you feel. The note is never answered by anyone. You were right to go.
You go and find the sender, which takes a month. It is a very frightened junior with a big idea. You send them home with a cup of tea and a long lecture.

events.text: The one above you on the Jade Register has held it a very long time, and has begun to make you a certain kind of conversation. It is the sort a person has with an heir. The Keeper of the Pillar watches the two of you from the shadow of the white pillar at the foot of the Stairs, who has not left the pillar in four hundred years. You realise it is an offer, and that no one will say so.

effects.log: You accept, quietly, by not refusing. It is a long, courteous, careful century, and you learn the weight of a place held above many others.

choices.text: Say you want it by your own hand

effects.log: You tell them you would sooner take it than be handed it. They smile as though they had been waiting centuries for someone to say that, and they let it lie.

events.text: The old holder of the first place makes an announcement: they will stand down, and there is no need to fight for it, the handover is arranged. Clerks of the Ministries are silent, the way people are when a long weather ends. The place is yours, with a slight air of having been laid on a tray.

choices.text: Take it, and keep their lessons

effects.log: You take it. It is a good place, and the old one is a good teacher, and the two things do not conflict as much as you feared.

choices.text: Ask them to keep it a decade more

effects.log: You ask them to keep it a decade more, to teach you the weight. They are touched and slightly alarmed, and the decade is the best of your life so far.

events.text: You take the first place the hard way, in front of clerks of the Ministries, against the one who held it, who goes at you without any softness at all. It is the most honest thing anyone has done for you in a thousand years. Afterwards they pour you tea and bow, once, from the waist.

choices.text: Bow back, to the same depth

effects.log: You bow back, to the same depth, and nobody on the isles will ever say the two of you were not equals at that moment.

choices.text: Ask them to teach you the rest

effects.log: You ask them to teach you the rest of what they know, which is a great deal. They agree, quietly. You get a decade of the best instruction on the isles.

You agree that you are, a good deal. They are delighted, and you part friends, and they will tell this version for the rest of their life.

choices.text: Take offence, a little, for show

effects.log: You take offence, a little, for show, and they are so horrified that you have to reassure them. It is the funniest part of your decade.

events.text: The Reckoning of Lamps brings back an old festival of yours, from before you came up, when it was smaller and you were poorer and the boiled eggs and bitter tea was a luxury. A man selling it at a stall has the same flat cap as the man then. It is almost certainly not him. You buy a portion anyway and sit down on a step to eat it.

effects.log: You eat it slowly, and it tastes smaller than you remember, and sweeter. For a few minutes you are who you were. Then you get up, and are who you are.

choices.text: Ask the vendor about the cap

effects.log: You ask the vendor about the cap. It was his grandfather's. He is touched you noticed, and gives you a second portion free.

choices.text: Give the portion to a child

effects.log: You give the second portion to a child who is eyeing it. They take it, without comment, as children do, and run. It is, you suspect, the correct ending.

events.text: A group of young immortals, new to the isles, are celebrating the Reckoning of Lamps with the intensity of people who do not yet know it comes every year. They ask you to join their circle. They have a game. They are very bad at it. They are very happy. You are suddenly a great deal older than you were an hour ago.

effects.log: You join the game, and are bad at it too, and it is the first time in years you have lost without minding. They will remember you as the immortal who played.
You teach them the old rules, which are better, and by the end of the night they have a new game, and you have a small following.
You watch from a distance, with a cup, and are warm in a way that has nothing to do with the cup. It is enough.

events.text: Somebody sets a lamp afloat at the Reckoning of Lamps with a name you know on it: someone who was a friend, long ago, and is not any more, of the ordinary kind of not. It is a lamp of the old type, cheap, paper, and a little crooked. It drifts to your side of the cloud and stays.

choices.text: Add a lamp of your own

effects.log: You add a lamp of your own, with nothing on it. The two drift off together. You tell nobody, and do not mind.

choices.text: Wave to the one who set it

effects.log: You look for whoever set it adrift, and find them, an old figure at the rail. You wave. They wave back. Neither of you moves from where you stand.
You let it go by. It is the kinder thing, and you tell yourself that, and the lamp is a small gold point on the cloud until it is gone.

events.text: It is customary at the Reckoning of Lamps to give small gifts, and somebody has given you one: a very small thing in a very large box, from a name that you do not know. Inside is a single dried boiled eggs and bitter tea-cake, wrapped in the red paper of the lowest isles, with a note: 'for the day you came up'. You were not aware anyone had been there.

effects.log: You keep the note, and the paper, and eat the cake the next morning. It is stale and wonderful. You never learn who sent it.
You find the sender, a young boy from the lowest isle, who watched you arrive and kept the memory for centuries, as the young do. You thank him in person, and he faints.
You send a gift in return, with no name, to the lowest isle. It is a good one. It is, you are told afterwards, the talk of three whole families.
